by: Claude Code (opus), titles and abstracts only

question.outcome: Iron or zinc status, deficiency or anaemia

decisions.reason: Pooled studies comparing serum ferritin (iron status) of adult vegetarians with non-vegetarian controls.
Meta-analysed zinc intake and serum zinc in people on vegetarian diets versus non-vegetarians, with vegan subgroups.
Compares vegetarian and non-vegetarian zinc intake and status, but only in pregnant women, a narrower group.

question.intervention: Phytate (phytic acid) in grains, beans, nuts and seeds, including foods treated to reduce it
question.outcome: Iron or zinc absorption, or iron and zinc status

decisions.reason: Reviews human studies comparing low- vs high-phytate breads (fermentation, phytase) on iron absorption and iron status, which matches every part of the question.
Pools isotope absorption studies in young children, relating the amount of phytate in the diet to zinc absorption; children are within the population.

question.intervention: Dietary fibre (apart from the phytate that often comes with it, where the review separates them)
question.outcome: Absorption or status of iron, zinc, calcium or magnesium

decisions.reason: Covers fibre-rich foods and prebiotics with iron and zinc outcomes, but only in people with celiac disease, and the comparison is not clearly less fibre.
Reviews clinical studies of dietary fibre types and their effect on iron absorption and iron status biomarkers in people.
Measures iron absorption and status, but uses prebiotic supplements or fortificants, often mixed with probiotics, in women and children only.
Measures iron status, but uses probiotic, prebiotic or synbiotic supplements, and only in people with anaemia.
Reports calcium and magnesium absorption, but uses inulin-type fructan supplements in healthy adults, and minerals are only one of many outcomes.
Reports calcium and magnesium absorption, but uses probiotic, prebiotic or synbiotic supplements in older adults and also includes animal studies.

question.intervention: Iron from meat and fish (haem iron)
question.comparison: Iron from plant foods or supplements (non-haem iron)

decisions.reason: Looks only at how bread fermentation and phytate reduction affect non-haem iron absorption; haem iron from meat or fish is never compared.
Compares haem with non-haem iron, but given as supplements rather than meat or fish, and it measures iron status rather than absorption.
The exposure is calcium intake and its effect on iron absorption, not haem iron compared with non-haem iron.
Compares diets with and without meat, but the outcome is serum ferritin (iron stores), not how much iron is absorbed.
Pools absorption studies to predict non-haem iron absorption from the food groups in a meal, but does not compare it with haem iron absorption.
Reviews iron absorption from whole diets, including enhancers, but reports only non-haem absorption with no haem comparison stated.

question.intervention: Plant protein (soy, pea, other plant sources or mixed plant foods)
question.outcome: Protein quality scores, muscle protein synthesis, lean mass or strength

decisions.reason: Network meta-analysis in healthy adults comparing plant proteins (pea, mycoprotein) with animal proteins (whey, egg) on muscle protein synthesis.
RCTs in adults aged 50 and over directly comparing plant with animal protein; pooled outcomes include lean mass and handgrip strength.
Young adults doing resistance training given soy or whey protein; outcomes are lean body mass, strength and plasma amino acids.
Compares soy with animal protein on body composition, but only in pre- and postmenopausal women, with a focus on adiposity.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing plant with animal protein on muscle mass, strength and physical performance.
Healthy people given plant protein vs other proteins (whey, beef, milk); outcomes include strength and muscle protein synthesis.
Adults given plant vs animal protein for at least 6 months; outcomes include lean body mass and muscle strength.
Compares plant proteins with whey in young adults, but the main focus is recovery from muscle damage; MPS is only one of the outcomes.
Older adults given soy protein, compared mainly with placebo or exercise; animal protein is only one of several control types.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing animal with plant protein on lean mass and muscle strength in adults.
Soy supplementation in athletes and active people aged 14 to 39; the comparison with whey on lean mass is only one part of the review.
Meta-analysis comparing soy with animal protein (whey, beef, milk, dairy) on lean body mass and strength during resistance training.
Compares whey and soy protein, but the outcome is inflammatory cytokines, not muscle or protein quality.
Compares animal with soy protein, but the outcomes are bone mineral density and bone markers, not muscle.

question.intervention: Meat, vitamin C, tea, coffee or calcium eaten with meals that contain plant iron
question.outcome: Iron absorption, or iron status over weeks or months

decisions.reason: Pools trials and crossover studies of dietary and supplemental calcium against lower calcium, with non-heme iron absorption and ferritin as outcomes.
Compares the iron status of vegetarians and non-vegetarians across whole diets, not meat added to plant-iron meals; most studies are cross-sectional.
Meta-analysis of meal absorption studies that models how food groups such as tea and cheese change non-heme iron absorption.
Vitamin C-rich fruits eaten with meals, with iron absorption and status as outcomes, but only in females and children, not all people.
Looks at eating more red meat and iron status over weeks in adults, not specifically meat eaten with plant-iron meals.
Vitamin C supplements given with iron supplements to people with anemia, not foods eaten with plant-iron meals.
Covers enhancers such as ascorbic acid and cow's milk with measured iron absorption, but only in children under 2 years.
Polyphenol supplements and iron status, rather than tea or coffee drunk with plant-iron meals.
Compares iron supplements against placebo in menstruating women, which is not the effect of foods eaten with plant-iron meals.
